terms.definition: A producer sends messages; a consumer receives and processes them. In pub-sub the producer is often called a publisher.
A named stream that publishers send messages to, without knowing who will read it.
The sender hands off a message and moves on, instead of waiting for the receiver to finish.

before.note: Read Message Queues first: pub-sub is the one-to-many shape of the same idea, and the delivery and ordering rules you learned there return here. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: A message queue hands each message to one consumer. Publish-subscribe is the other shape: a publisher sends a message to a topic, and the topic delivers a copy to every interested reader. The publisher does not know, and does not need to know, who those readers are. Google describes its Pub/Sub service as an asynchronous messaging service that decouples the services producing messages from the services processing them [[gcp-pubsub-overview]].

The point of this is loose coupling. When one order event matters to billing, email and analytics all at once, calling each system in turn ties them together: the order service must know every reader, and a slow reader slows the order. Publishing one message to a topic instead lets each reader take its own copy at its own pace, and lets you add a new reader later without touching the publisher [[sns-dg]].

Delivering one message to many endpoints is called fan-out. Amazon's SNS puts it plainly: a topic acts as a logical access point, and a fanout scenario is when a message published to a topic is replicated and pushed to multiple endpoints such as queues, functions and HTTP endpoints [[sns-dg]]. That one-to-many delivery is the whole difference from a plain queue.

terms.definition: A pattern where each message sent to a topic is delivered to every interested subscriber, not just one consumer.
The sender that puts a message on a topic without knowing who reads it.
A reader that registers interest in a topic and receives its messages.
Delivering one published message to many endpoints at once.
Letting the publisher and its readers run, fail and scale independently by communicating through a topic.

stages.name: How it works
body: Readers attach to a topic through a subscription. Each subscription is one reader's own view of the topic, with its own position and its own backlog, and every subscription receives every message. Google Pub/Sub splits the two ways a subscriber can get messages: in a pull subscription the subscriber asks for messages, and in a push subscription the service sends each message to an endpoint the subscriber gave [[gcp-pubsub-sub]].

Inside a single subscription, several workers can share the load, so each message goes to just one of them. This is the queue behaviour living inside pub-sub: separate subscriptions each get a full copy, while workers in one subscription divide that subscription's messages. It is how you broadcast to many systems and still scale any one of them.

Delivery is confirmed by acknowledgement. A subscriber receives a message, does the work, and acknowledges it; if it does not acknowledge in time, the message is delivered again. Because a crash between work and acknowledgement causes a repeat, the default is at-least-once delivery, and subscribers must be safe to process the same message twice. Google Pub/Sub offers an exactly-once option, but the baseline every design should assume is at-least-once [[gcp-pubsub-sub]].

Order is not global. Kafka keeps order only inside one partition: it guarantees that any consumer of a given topic-partition reads that partition's events in exactly the same order they were written [[kafka-intro]]. Google Pub/Sub reaches the same place with ordering keys: an ordering key is a string identifying related messages that should be ordered, such as a customer ID, and messages with an empty ordering key are not ordered [[gcp-pubsub-order]]. Either way, if two events must stay in sequence, give them the same key.

terms.definition: One reader's view of a topic, with its own position and backlog; every subscription gets every message.
In a pull subscription the subscriber requests messages; in a push subscription the service delivers them to an endpoint.
A subscriber's signal that it finished a message; without one in time, the message is redelivered.
Every message arrives, possibly more than once, so subscribers must be idempotent.
A value that keeps related messages in order by routing them together; messages with no key are unordered.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: A message that cannot be processed must not block the ones behind it. The usual fix is a dead-letter queue: after a set number of failed deliveries the message is set aside for inspection or replay. Amazon SNS defines it as an Amazon SQS queue that a subscription can target for messages that can't be delivered successfully, and says that once the retries in the retry policy are exhausted, SNS discards the message unless such a dead-letter queue is attached [[sns-dg]].

Because delivery is at-least-once, duplicates are a fact of life, so subscribers should be idempotent: handling the same message twice has the same effect as once. The common technique is to record each message's unique id and skip one you have already handled. Google Pub/Sub can be configured for exactly-once delivery, but it is the stronger, more expensive mode; the safe default is to design the subscriber to tolerate a repeat [[gcp-pubsub-sub]].

Ordering is a trade-off, not a free guarantee. Keeping related messages in order means routing them to the same partition or ordering key, which limits how much you can parallelise them, since one key's messages are processed in sequence. Unrelated messages, with different keys, still run in parallel. So you order only what truly needs it and let everything else fan out freely [[gcp-pubsub-order]].

terms.definition: A place a message is moved to after repeated failures, so it stops blocking the messages behind it.
The rule for how many times, and how often, a failed delivery is retried before the message is dropped or dead-lettered.
A subscriber for which handling the same message twice has the same effect as handling it once.
A stronger, costlier mode that removes duplicates; most designs instead assume at-least-once and deduplicate.
One stuck message holding up every message behind it until it is parked or dropped.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The two mental models in the field map onto two product shapes. A log like Kafka keeps a retained, ordered record per partition, so many subscribers can read, re-read and replay the same history at their own offsets [[kafka-intro]]. A managed topic like Google Pub/Sub or Amazon SNS pushes or serves copies to subscriptions and endpoints and handles retries and dead-lettering for you [[sns-dg]]. Both are pub-sub; they differ in whether the history is a durable log you seek within or a stream you acknowledge and move past.

Pub-sub is powerful but adds operational surface. Each subscription is its own backlog that can fall behind, each needs its own alerting, and a topic with hundreds of event types becomes something to name, monitor and clean up. The failure mode is rarely a lost message; it is a quietly growing backlog on one subscription while the others look fine, so per-subscription lag is the thing to watch.

Correctness changes too. Publishing an event means the work finishes some time after the publisher returns, so anything the publisher must know immediately, such as whether stock exists, still needs a direct call. Combined with at-least-once delivery, idempotent subscribers and a dead-letter queue for poison messages, this is the standard way large systems broadcast events while staying decoupled, which is why pub-sub sits at the messaging end of this map, just past queues [[gcp-pubsub-overview]].

terms.definition: A subscriber's position in a log such as Kafka, which it advances as it reads and can rewind to replay.
Reading a retained log again from an earlier position, which a durable log allows but a plain acknowledged stream does not.
How far behind the latest message a subscription is; growing lag signals a backlog on that reader alone.
Work finishing after the publisher returns, which callers that need an immediate answer must design around.

misconceptions.myth: Every subscriber shares one copy of each message, like a queue.
misconceptions.truth: Every subscription receives every message; only workers inside one subscription share its messages [[gcp-pubsub-sub]].

misconceptions.myth: Messages always arrive in the order they were published.
misconceptions.truth: Order is kept only within a partition, or for messages with the same ordering key; an empty ordering key means no order [[gcp-pubsub-order]].

misconceptions.myth: A topic guarantees each message is processed exactly once.
misconceptions.truth: The default is at-least-once delivery, so a message can arrive twice and subscribers must be idempotent [[gcp-pubsub-sub]].

misconceptions.myth: A message that keeps failing just gets retried until it works.
misconceptions.truth: After the retry policy is exhausted the message is dropped unless a dead-letter queue is attached to catch it [[sns-dg]].
